title: The statmodels7 Framework
text:
Preface
This book is the mathematical companion to the statmodels7 toolkit. Its purpose is to collect in one place the mathematics that the packages implement. That covers the link functions with their derivatives to fourth order, the probability distributions with their scores and information matrices, the operations that build new distributions out of existing ones, and the optimisation methods that fit them.
It is written to be taught from as much as to be consulted, and that has settled two questions of style. The first is what to show. Every formula the toolkit actually evaluates appears on the page, in the form the code uses, together with enough of the reasoning to make it intelligible: where a quantity comes from, what it means, and which condition it depends on. What does not appear is the formal proof. A reader who wants the argument in full is pointed to the paper or the textbook where it is given properly, and the appendix collects those references. The space this saves is spent on explaining the results and the places where the implementation had to make a choice. The second question is how to say it. The mathematics here is elementary throughout — calculus, a little probability, the occasional exchange of derivative and integral — and the prose aims to be continuous and unhurried rather than clipped, so that the chapters can be read straight through.
The mathematics is not new, and no attempt is made to pretend otherwise. What is particular to this book is that the formulas shown are the formulas the packages run, which is a claim about software rather than about mathematics, and whose value rests on the care taken to keep it true.
The book is generated with Quarto directly from the source code of the packages, which are loaded from the working tree each time it is rendered. The numerical examples scattered through the chapters are therefore executed by the very code they illustrate, and the output shown is the output produced at build time.

title: The statmodels7 Framework
text:
How the book is organised
After the introduction there is one chapter per package, so that the book grows the way the toolkit does.
1  Introduction explains what the toolkit is for and why it is built the way it is. It contains no mathematics and can be read on its own.
2  The linkfunctions7 package is linkfunctions7: what a link is required to satisfy, how the derivatives of a link and of its inverse determine one another, and why they are carried to fourth order. It ends with a catalogue of the sixteen link classes, each with its formulas written out in full.
3  The distributions7 package is distributions7, and divides into five. Distributions develops the likelihood theory the toolkit rests on — score, observed and expected information, the Bartlett identities, derivatives on the unconstrained scale via Faà di Bruno’s formula, derivatives of the distribution function — and presents the fourteen families. Particular care is taken where the parametrisation differs from the one used by base R. Transformations of distributions treats the operations that turn one distribution into another, and is the most demanding part of the book, since the wrappers compose with any parent and their formulas are therefore stated once, in general, at every order the toolkit supports. Fitting a distribution fits a distribution to a sample by maximum likelihood, which is the smallest problem that exercises all of the preceding machinery at once. Numerical fallbacks describes what a distribution receives when it implements nothing but its density. Several dimensions treats families whose observations are vectors, where the likelihood theory is unchanged and only the parametrisation of the matrix has to be arranged.
4  The optimizers7 package is optimizers7, and divides into four as well. Descent directions and line searches defines descent directions and the conditions a line search must guarantee. Second-order and quasi-Newton methods takes the methods in order of how much curvature they store, from the exact Hessian down to a single number. Non-smooth objectives deals with objectives that have a kink, where the gradient does not become small at the solution and a gradient-based method reaches the answer and reports failure. Box constraints and stochastic gradients covers box constraints, removed by a change of variable, and Adam, whose steps are not descent steps. Finally Starting values and multiple starts covers the choice of the starting point, which reuses the same change of variable, and the question of how many runs to make.
5  The basis7 package is basis7, and divides into five. Basis expansions defines a basis expansion and the four quantities the package computes from it. The three families presents B-splines, the Fourier basis and the Legendre polynomials, each generated by a recurrence that also produces its derivatives and its integral. Inner products is about the matrix of inner products, which a roughness penalty is a quadratic form in and which is computed exactly rather than approximated on a grid. Linear transformations of a basis derives the three linear transformations of a basis — orthonormalisation, a linear constraint, and the Demmler-Reinsch construction — from the property each is asked to produce. Bases of several variables builds a basis of several variables from marginal ones.
6  The covstructs7 package is covstructs7, and divides into three. Matrix parameters sets out what a matrix parameter is and why it is not a link. The families presents the log-Cholesky map, the diagonal families that reuse the link functions of 2  The linkfunctions7 package, and the fixed matrix carried by a single scale. Rank and the null space treats matrices that are not of full rank, which is what a penalty is, and the pseudo-determinant and rank determination they require.
Appendix A — Notation collects the notation used throughout, and the references follow it.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Duplicated infrastructure
Almost every R modelling package contains, somewhere in its internals, its own private copy of the Gamma distribution, written as a handful of helper functions. Typically there is a switch on a character string that returns a density, a closure that computes a score, and a block inside a fitting routine that produces the one second derivative that routine needs. The same is true of link functions. Every package that fits something positive carries its own log link, and every package that fits a probability carries its own logit.
None of these objects can be reused, because none of them is really an object. They are code paths, private to the package that owns them, and they contain only what their author’s routine happened to call for — usually the density and the score, sometimes the Hessian, almost never anything beyond. A package that needs a third derivative writes its own Gamma from scratch; a package that wants derivatives with respect to an unconstrained parameter does the same. The result is that the R ecosystem contains dozens of Gamma distributions, each partial and each capable of being wrong in its own way.
The observation the toolkit is built on is that all of this is unnecessary, because a Gamma distribution is a fixed mathematical object. It does not vary from package to package. Its density, score, information, third and fourth derivatives, derivatives with respect to the response and behaviour under reparametrisation are all determined by the definition, once and for all. They can therefore be written down once, correctly and completely, for everyone to build on.
That is what statmodels7 is: infrastructure meant to be reused, rather than another modelling package. The measure of its success is not how well it fits models but whether somebody else’s modelling package can be built on top of it.

title: 1  Introduction
section: 1.2 The contents of a complete implementation
text:
1.2 The contents of a complete implementation
The principle applies to both kinds of object the toolkit currently provides, and it takes a different form for each, because what counts as complete differs.
A link function is a map between a constrained parameter and an unconstrained one, and what a modelling routine can ask of it is its value and its derivatives — in both directions. Almost every implementation in R carries the first derivative of the inverse link and stops there, which is exactly what a GLM fitted by iterative least squares needs and nothing more. A link in this toolkit carries four derivatives of the forward map and four of the inverse, so it can serve a routine working at any order up to the fourth. It also knows its own domain, so the routine does not have to.
A distribution supplies, or can derive, the following. It has the density or mass function, the cdf, the quantile function and a random generator. It has the score, the observed information and the expected information, plus third and fourth derivatives of the log-likelihood, both observed and expected. It has derivatives with respect to the response as well as the parameters, and derivatives of the distribution function, which is what a censored observation contributes. Finally, it provides every one of these with respect to the unconstrained parameters as well as the natural ones.
The items at the end of each list are the ones usually missing elsewhere, and they are precisely the ones a modelling framework depends on. Derivatives in the response are what quantile-type residuals and smoothness penalties are made of. Derivatives on the unconstrained scale are what an optimiser wants: a Gamma variance must stay positive, and an algorithm forced to respect that constraint is doing constrained optimisation, whereas an algorithm working with \(\eta = \log \sigma^2\) moves freely over the whole real line. Third and fourth derivatives, finally, are the raw material of higher-order asymptotics and bias correction.
This is also where the two packages meet, and why neither would be much use alone. Transporting a fourth derivative of a log-likelihood from the natural scale to the unconstrained one is an application of Faà di Bruno’s formula, and it consumes exactly the four derivatives of the inverse link that linkfunctions7 carries — Section 3.1.4 works this out in detail. A link stopping at second order would silently cap the whole toolkit at second-order methods, however much the distributions knew about themselves.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 The toolkit
The name encodes a convention: every package name ends in 7, the 7 being the S7 object system everything is built on.

The toolkit






Package
What it provides




linkfunctions7
16 link classes with exact analytical derivatives to fourth order, in both directions


distributions7
14 distributions with exact score, information and third/fourth derivatives, plus wrappers, transformations and maximum likelihood


optimizers7
11 optimisation algorithms as objects, with composable stopping rules, safeguards that report themselves, starting values generated on the unconstrained scale, and box constraints removed by reparameterisation


basis7
bases as objects: evaluation, derivatives of any order, the integral anchored at the lower endpoint, and exact inner products; B-splines, Fourier and Legendre, products of them for several variables, and the linear transformations that orthonormalise, constrain and diagonalise


covstructs7
constrained matrix parameters: a map from an unconstrained vector to a symmetric matrix, exact to second order, with the log-determinant and the solves; rank-deficient matrices admitted, since that is what a penalty is


modelterms7
planned — model terms usable directly in formulas


penalties7
planned — penalties


statmodels7
planned — the modelling framework itself



The destination is the last row: a framework in the spirit of the generalized additive models for location, scale and shape of Rigby and Stasinopoulos (2005), described at length in Stasinopoulos et al. (2017). In that framework every parameter of a distribution can be modelled rather than just the mean, the optimiser is pluggable, and estimation can be frequentist or Bayesian. Users can also define new model terms and drop them straight into formulas. Everything below it exists to make that possible, and one design pressure has shaped it all: exact derivatives, on the unconstrained scale, for components the framework has never seen before.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Extending the toolkit
A toolkit that worked only for the sixteen links and fourteen distributions it ships with would have solved nothing; it would simply be one more closed catalogue, larger than the others. What matters is what happens when a user brings an object the authors never considered. In both packages the object is treated exactly like the ones that came with them: there is no registration step and no separate interface for the “advanced” case.
For a link the requirement is only that the ten generics be implemented, and since a link is a formula and its derivatives, that is a dozen lines. Nothing distinguishes the result from a built-in one: it can be handed to any distribution as the link for any parameter, and the fourth-order machinery will use it without knowing where it came from.

NegLog <- S7::new_class("NegLog", parent = link, package = NULL)

S7::method(linkfun,   NegLog) <- function(x, theta) -log(theta)
S7::method(linkinv,   NegLog) <- function(x, eta)   exp(-eta)
S7::method(dlinkfun,  NegLog) <- function(x, theta) -1 / theta
S7::method(d2linkfun, NegLog) <- function(x, theta)  1 / theta^2
S7::method(dlinkinv,  NegLog) <- function(x, eta)   -exp(-eta)
S7::method(d2linkinv, NegLog) <- function(x, eta)    exp(-eta)

neglog <- NegLog(link_name = "neglog", link_bounds = c(0, Inf), link_params = NULL)
linkinv(neglog, linkfun(neglog, c(0.5, 2)))
#> [1] 0.5 2.0

For a distribution the contract is even smaller, and it is the one that decides whether the package is infrastructure or a catalogue: a new distribution needs nothing but its density. Everything else has a fallback — the cdf is computed by quadrature, the quantile function by root-finding, the random generator by a ratio-of-uniforms scheme that needs only the density, and every derivative by finite differences. Whatever the user later supplies in closed form simply replaces the corresponding fallback, with no registration step and no separate interface for the “advanced” case.
To see what this means in practice, here is a complete definition of the Rayleigh distribution, which has density \(f(y;\sigma) = (y/\sigma^2)\, e^{-y^2/2\sigma^2}\) on \((0, \infty)\):

Rayleigh <- S7::new_class("Rayleigh", parent = continuous_distrib, package = NULL)

S7::method(distrib_pdf, Rayleigh) <- function(distrib, y, theta, log = FALSE) {
  s <- theta[[1]]
  ld <- log(y) - 2 * log(s) - y^2 / (2 * s^2)
  if (log) ld else exp(ld)
}

rayleigh <- Rayleigh(
  distrib_name = "rayleigh", dimension = "univariate", bounds = c(0, Inf),
  params = "sigma", params_interpretation = c(sigma = "scale"), n_params = 1,
  params_bounds = list(sigma = c(0, Inf)),
  link_params = list(sigma = log_link())
)

Nothing above mentions a cdf, a quantile function, a generator or a derivative, and yet all of them are immediately available. The median of a Rayleigh is \(\sigma\sqrt{2\log 2}\), its score is \(y^2/\sigma^3 - 2/\sigma\), and its expected information is \(4/\sigma^2\); the fallbacks recover each of these from the density alone:

theta <- list(sigma = 2)

distrib_quantile(rayleigh, 0.5, theta)     # by root-finding on the numerical cdf
#> [1] 2.35482
2 * sqrt(2 * log(2))                       # the closed form
#> [1] 2.35482

distrib_gradient(rayleigh, c(1, 3), theta) # by finite differences
#> $sigma
#> [1] -0.875  0.125
c(1, 3)^2 / 2^3 - 2 / 2                    # the closed form
#> [1] -0.875  0.125

distrib_expected_hessian(rayleigh, 1, theta)$sigma_sigma   # -4/sigma^2
#> [1] -1

The twenty lines above are a first-class citizen of the toolkit: the object can be zero-inflated, truncated, transformed, and fitted by Fisher scoring exactly like the distributions the package ships with.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.5 Validators
Because users are expected to write their own distributions and links, the packages ship the tools to validate them. check_link() verifies that a link is invertible in both directions, strictly monotone and consistent with the inverse function theorem, and that each analytical derivative agrees with a numerical one. check_distrib() runs the analogous battery on a distribution. It checks that the density integrates to one, that the cdf and the quantile function invert each other and agree with the density, and that the random generator matches the cdf. It also checks every derivative against a finite-difference computation, and the expected information against a Monte Carlo estimate of the variance of the score.
Both run on any object, including one just defined — here, on the two objects above:

invisible(check_link(neglog))
#> Checking S7 Link Object: neglog 
#>   [1] Invertibility (Theta space): [PASSED] 
#>   [2] Invertibility (Eta space):   [PASSED] 
#>   [3] Strict Monotonicity:         [PASSED] 
#>   [4] Inverse Function Theorem:    [PASSED] 
#>   [5] Link Derivatives:            [PASSED to order 2, 2 numerical] 
#>   [6] Inverse Link Derivatives:    [PASSED to order 2, 2 numerical]


res <- check_distrib(rayleigh, theta = list(sigma = 2), orders = 1:2,
                     nsim = 5e4, verbose = FALSE)
res[, c("check", "status")]
#>                                         check status
#> 1                     density integrates to 1     OK
#> 2                     density is non-negative     OK
#> 3             cdf in [0,1] and non-decreasing     OK
#> 4                 cdf agrees with the density     OK
#> 5                     quantile/cdf round-trip     OK
#> 6                         rng matches the cdf     OK
#> 7              gradient vs finite differences     OK
#> 8               hessian vs finite differences     OK
#> 9         expected information vs Monte Carlo     OK
#> 10 response derivatives vs finite differences     OK
#> 11  link-scale gradient vs finite differences     OK

The link above declares only two derivative orders of the four, and the validator says so rather than passing what it was not given.
basis7 ships check_basis(), which does the same for a basis and reports a quantity it cannot check independently as unchecked rather than as passed.
The validators are used systematically on everything the packages contain. The five chapters that follow present the mathematics behind all of it, one per package: Chapter 2 for linkfunctions7, Chapter 3 for distributions7, Chapter 4 for optimizers7, Chapter 5 for basis7, and Chapter 6 for covstructs7.




Rigby, Robert A., and D. Mikis Stasinopoulos. 2005. “Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape.” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C 54 (3): 507–54.


Stasinopoulos, D. Mikis, Robert A. Rigby, Gillian Z. Heller, Vlasios Voudouris, and Fernanda De Bastiani. 2017. Flexible Regression and Smoothing: Using GAMLSS in R. Boca Raton: Chapman; Hall/CRC.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text:
2.1 Definition
The parameters of a distribution are usually constrained: a scale is positive, a probability lies between zero and one, a correlation between minus one and one. An optimiser, on the other hand, works best with an argument it can move freely in any direction. A link function connects the two: it maps the constrained domain of a parameter onto an unconstrained scale, and its inverse maps the optimiser’s iterates back into the domain where the distribution is defined. This chapter gives the precise definition, derives the relationship between the derivatives of a link and those of its inverse, explains why the toolkit carries both to fourth order, and ends with the catalogue of the sixteen link classes that linkfunctions7 provides.
Three observations about this definition are useful before going on.
First, the definition does not require \(g\) to be increasing. Since \(g'\) is continuous and never zero on an interval, \(g\) is automatically strictly monotone, but the direction can be either, and both directions occur in practice: the link for a parameter bounded above, \(g(\theta) = \log(u -
\theta)\), is strictly decreasing. Code that assumes an increasing link, for example when mapping the endpoints of an interval through it, fails on this case. The property to require and to test is therefore strict monotonicity of either sign.
Second, the image \(E\) need not be the whole real line. For the square-root link \(E = (0, \infty)\), and the same holds for the reciprocal link. In these cases the optimiser is not fully unconstrained, because the constraint has moved from \(\theta\) to \(\eta\), and an optimiser can still step outside the domain and receive NaN. For this reason the catalogue below states \(E\) explicitly for every link.
Third, the definition requires four continuous derivatives instead of the customary one or two. The link objects in stats::make.link() carry the first derivative of the inverse and nothing else, because a generalized linear model fitted by iteratively reweighted least squares needs nothing more. This is the setting of Nelder and Wedderburn (1972) and McCullagh and Nelder (1989), where the link function first appears under that name. This toolkit needs more: as Section 3.1.4 shows, transporting a fourth-order derivative of a log-likelihood onto the unconstrained scale requires \(h'\), \(h''\), \(h'''\) and \(h''''\), so a link that stopped at second order would restrict the entire toolkit to second-order methods.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text: Definition 2.1 (Link function) Let \(\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be an open interval. A link function on \(\Theta\) is a map \(g : \Theta \to \mathbb{R}\) which is a bijection onto its image \(E = g(\Theta)\), itself an open interval; which is four times continuously differentiable on \(\Theta\); and which is regular, meaning that \(g'(\theta) \neq 0\) everywhere. We write \(h = g^{-1} : E \to \Theta\) for the inverse, and throughout the book \(\eta = g(\theta)\) and \(\theta = h(\eta)\).

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text:
2.2 Derivatives of the inverse link
Every link in the catalogue implements two families of derivatives: those of \(g\) with respect to \(\theta\), and those of \(h\) with respect to \(\eta\). Each family determines the other completely, and the formulas that connect them are used throughout the toolkit.

Theorem 2.1 (Derivatives of an inverse function) Let \(g\) be a link function in the sense of Definition 2.1 and let \(h = g^{-1}\). Then, with every derivative of \(g\) evaluated at \(\theta = h(\eta)\),
\[
h' = \frac{1}{g'}, \qquad
h'' = -\frac{g''}{(g')^{3}}, \qquad
h''' = \frac{3(g'')^{2} - g'g'''}{(g')^{5}}, \qquad
h'''' = \frac{-15(g'')^{3} + 10\,g'g''g''' - (g')^{2}g''''}{(g')^{7}}.
\]

All four expressions follow from the identity \(h(g(\theta)) = \theta\), which holds for every \(\theta\) in the domain because \(h\) is the inverse of \(g\). Differentiating this identity once gives \(h'\,g' = 1\), and hence the first formula. Each further differentiation produces an equation that is linear in the highest derivative of \(h\), with a power of \(g'\) as its coefficient; since \(g'\) never vanishes, this equation can be solved for that derivative, and the remaining formulas follow one after another. The same procedure, carried to arbitrary order and organised through set partitions, is the Faà di Bruno formula, whose history and combinatorics are presented in Johnson (2002) and Comtet (1974). Section 3.1.4 uses it in that general form to transport likelihood derivatives of any order onto the unconstrained scale.
A short example makes the formulas concrete and checks the signs. For the log link, \(g(\theta) = \log\theta\), the inverse \(h(\eta) = e^\eta\) is its own derivative at every order, so every \(h^{(k)}\) must equal \(u = e^{\eta} = \theta\). On the forward side \(g' = u^{-1}\), \(g'' = -u^{-2}\), \(g''' = 2u^{-3}\) and \(g'''' = -6u^{-4}\). Substituting into the fourth formula,
\[\frac{-15(-u^{-2})^{3} + 10\,u^{-1}(-u^{-2})(2u^{-3}) - u^{-2}(-6u^{-4})}{u^{-7}}
= \frac{15u^{-6} - 20u^{-6} + 6u^{-6}}{u^{-7}} = u,\]
which is the correct value.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
section: 2.3 The role of the fourth order
text:
2.3 The role of the fourth order
The fourth derivative of a link is genuinely used, and the formula derived in Section 3.1.4 for the fourth derivative of a log-likelihood with respect to the linear predictor shows where:
\[
\frac{\partial^{4}\ell}{\partial\eta^{4}}
= \ell^{(\theta\theta\theta\theta)}(h')^{4}
+ 6\,\ell^{(\theta\theta\theta)}(h')^{2}h''
+ \ell^{(\theta\theta)}\left(4h'h''' + 3(h'')^{2}\right)
+ \ell^{(\theta)}\,h'''' .
\]
The last term contains \(h''''\), which vanishes only for an affine link. A link implemented only to second order would therefore make this quantity wrong, not merely less accurate, and the error would not shrink as the sample grows. Fourth-order likelihood derivatives are exactly what bias correction and higher-order asymptotics require, so the four-derivative requirement in Definition 2.1 is necessary for those applications.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text:
2.4 The interface
A link is an S7 object. The base class link carries the name, the domain \(\Theta\) (link_bounds), and any additional parameters the link needs, such as the exponent of the power link; each concrete link is a subclass.

lk <- logit_link()
lk
#> S7 Link Object: logit
#>   - Parameter domain (theta): (0, 1)
c(lk@link_name, lk@link_bounds)
#> [1] "logit" "0"     "1"

Every link implements the same ten generics, five in each direction:

The ten generics


Generic
Returns




linkfun(x, theta)
\(g(\theta)\)


linkinv(x, eta)
\(h(\eta)\)


dlinkfun … d4linkfun
\(g'(\theta)\) … \(g''''(\theta)\)


dlinkinv … d4linkinv
\(h'(\eta)\) … \(h''''(\eta)\)



For interactive work, two routers select the order at run time:

theta <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)
linkfun(lk, theta)
#> [1] -1.386294  0.000000  1.386294
linkderiv(lk, theta, order = 2)
#> [1] -23.4375   0.0000  23.4375
linkinvderiv(lk, linkfun(lk, theta), order = 2)
#> [1]  0.096  0.000 -0.096

One practical remark about these routers. linkderiv() dispatches on the link and then calls the order-specific generic, which dispatches again. An S7 dispatch costs roughly five microseconds, against one microsecond for a plain call, so the second dispatch accounts for about a third of the total. The cost accumulates in a loop: distributions7 evaluates inverse-link derivatives once per parameter per order on every scoring iteration. Performance-critical code therefore calls dlinkinv() and its siblings directly, and the routers are intended for interactive use.
Every link also carries print and plot methods. The plot draws the two directions of the map side by side: the forward direction stretches the neighbourhoods of the domain’s endpoints out to infinity, and the inverse compresses the whole real line back between them.

plot(cloglog_link())




The complementary log-log link, in both directions.

title: 2  The linkfunctions7 package
text:
2.5 The catalogue
Fourteen constructors produce sixteen classes: bounded_link() returns a lower-, an upper- or a doubly-bounded link according to which of its two arguments are supplied, and reduces to the identity link when neither is. For each entry the table gives the domain, the pair \(g\) and \(h\), and all eight derivatives; the accompanying note records the mathematical or numerical properties specific to that link. Links that take a parameter — the power link, the softplus, the bounded family — are shown at a representative value.


2.5.1 Identity
identity_link()
Domain: \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\), so that \(\eta \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[g(\theta) = \theta, \qquad h(\eta) = \eta\]

The trivial case, kept as an object so that a parameter that needs no transformation is still described by the same interface as one that does.


2.5.2 Log
log_link()
Domain: \(\theta \in (0, \infty)\), so that \(\eta \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[g(\theta) = \log\theta, \qquad h(\eta) = e^{\eta}\]

Log: derivatives to fourth order


\(k\)

1

In general \(g^{(k)}(\theta) = (-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!\,\theta^{-k}\), and the inverse is its own derivative to every order. The implementation floors \(h\) and its derivatives at a small positive value, since a large negative \(\eta\) would otherwise underflow to exactly zero and the subsequent \(1/\theta\) return Inf. Where to put that floor is decided by the highest forward derivative carried, \(-6/\theta^{4}\): the floor is the smallest value keeping it finite, which is near \(10^{-77}\) rather than anywhere near machine epsilon, so \(\theta\) stays exact down to \(\eta \approx -177\).


2.5.3 Square root
sqrt_link()
Domain: \(\theta \in (0, \infty)\), so that \(\eta \in (0, \infty)\).
\[g(\theta) = \sqrt{\theta}, \qquad h(\eta) = \eta^{2}\]
