title: 6  The covstructs7 package
text:
6.1 Matrix parameters
Chapter 2 describes how a constrained scalar is carried onto the real line by a link function. A modelling toolkit meets constrained matrices as well: the covariance of a multivariate response, the precision of a random effect, the penalty matrix of a smooth term. This chapter presents the objects covstructs7 uses for them, and explains why they are a separate construction rather than a matrix-valued link.
The mathematics of differentiating a function of a matrix with respect to a parametrisation of that matrix is classical, and Magnus and Neudecker (1999) is the standard reference. The unconstrained parametrisations themselves come from Pinheiro and Bates (1996), whose paper is the origin of the log-Cholesky map used here, and Pourahmadi (2011) reviews the field.
Section 6.1 sets out what a structure is: a map from an unconstrained vector to a symmetric matrix, the derivatives of that map, and the four quantities a likelihood asks of the matrix it produces. It explains why the Jacobian of such a map is not diagonal and why that single fact rules out treating the construction as a link.
Section 6.2 presents the families the package ships. The log-Cholesky map is the general positive definite case, and its log-determinant turns out to be linear in the free vector. The diagonal families are where this package composes with linkfunctions7 rather than competing with it. The scaled fixed matrix is the case a penalty needs, and it is the reason the package admits matrices that are not of full rank.
Section 6.3 is about those. A rank-deficient matrix is not a defect here but the definition of a penalty, and the section explains what has to change to accommodate one: the determinant becomes a pseudo-determinant, the inverse becomes a solve restricted to the range, and the rank itself has to be determined in a way that does not depend on the arithmetic that produced the matrix.

title: 6  The covstructs7 package
text:
6.1.1 The map and its free vector
Let \(\mathcal{M}\) be a set of symmetric \(p \times p\) matrices defined by a constraint: positive definite matrices, positive definite matrices with a prescribed pattern of zeros, correlation matrices, or positive semidefinite matrices of a fixed null space. A structure is a map
\[
M : \mathbb{R}^{d} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}, \qquad \eta \longmapsto M(\eta),
\tag{6.1}\]
whose image is the whole of \(\mathcal{M}\) and which is one-to-one, together with the derivatives of that map and the quantities a likelihood asks of its value. The vector \(\eta\) is called free because it carries no constraint: every point of \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) is admissible, and an optimiser may take any step from any point without leaving the domain. This is the same bargain a link function offers for a scalar, and for the same reason: the constraint is absorbed into the map so that the estimation problem is unconstrained.
The number \(d\) of free values is the dimension of \(\mathcal{M}\) as a manifold, not \(p^2\) or \(p(p+1)/2\) in general. A full positive definite matrix has \(d = p(p+1)/2\); a diagonal one has \(d = p\); a matrix that is a fixed matrix times an unknown scale has \(d = 1\). A structure therefore owns its dimension: a map for \(3 \times 3\) matrices and a map for \(4 \times 4\) matrices are different objects, with different \(d\) and different names for the free values, and both are needed before any data exist because they determine the shape of the parameter vector.
Each free value carries a label, and the labels are fixed at construction. The distribution of Section 3.5 builds its parameter names from them, the derivative components of the likelihood are keyed by them, and the printed summary of a fit reports them, so they are part of the interface rather than a convenience.


6.1.2 Why this is not a link
A link function of Chapter 2 is a scalar map \(g\) applied to each parameter separately. Applied to a vector of parameters, it produces a diagonal Jacobian, which is what makes the chain rule of Section 3.1.4 factorise: the \(k\)th derivative in the \(k\)th direction involves only \(h^{(j)}\) for that one coordinate, and Faà di Bruno’s formula reduces to a product of partial Bell polynomials in one variable.
A matrix parametrisation has no such structure. Changing one free value of a log-Cholesky map changes an entire row and column of the matrix it produces, so \(\partial M / \partial \eta_k\) is a matrix rather than a number and the Jacobian \(\partial \mathrm{vech}(M) / \partial \eta\) is dense. The chain rule still holds, but it is a matrix chain rule, and the quantities a consumer needs from it are traces rather than products. Nothing that linkfunctions7 computes would be reusable, and a consumer that treated a matrix parametrisation as a link would be wrong in a way that produces plausible numbers.
The two constructions therefore stay apart, and meet at the one place where they agree, which is a diagonal matrix. There the Jacobian is diagonal, and covstructs7 reuses the link objects exactly as they are rather than writing its own positive maps; see Section 6.2.2.


6.1.3 What a consumer asks
A likelihood that carries a matrix parameter asks four things of it, and a structure answers all four.
The matrix itself, \(M(\eta)\), is the only compulsory one; everything else has a numerical method available from it alone.
The derivatives \(A_k = \partial M/\partial \eta_k\) and \(A_{kl} = \partial^2 M/\partial \eta_k \partial \eta_l\) are what the score and the observed information of Section 3.5.2 are built from. Only the \(d(d+1)/2\) distinct second derivatives are computed, keyed by the same enumeration that names them. Recovering an index by splitting a name on its separator is the obvious route and it is wrong, since a free value whose own label contains the separator splits into the wrong number of pieces; the package generates indices and names from one enumeration so that the two cannot disagree.
The log-determinant \(\log|M|\) and its first two derivatives are the normalising constant of a gaussian and its derivatives. The identity behind them is
\[
\frac{\partial \log|M|}{\partial \eta_k}
  = \mathrm{tr}\!\left(M^{-1} A_k\right),
\tag{6.2}\]
which is Magnus and Neudecker (1999)’s, and which makes a closed-form log-determinant derivative something other than an independent claim: it must agree with the derivative of the matrix through Equation 6.2, and the package’s validator compares the two routes.
The solve \(M^{-1}B\) is what a quadratic form needs. It is computed through a factorisation rather than by forming an inverse, which is both cheaper and better conditioned; a family that knows its own factor supplies it, and the rest obtain one from the matrix.

s <- covstructs7::log_cholesky(3)
s
#> Structure: log_cholesky
#> Matrix:    3 x 3, symmetric
#> Rank:      3 of 3
#> Role:      either
#> 
#> Free values: 6
#>   log_L1, log_L2, log_L3, L2.1, L3.1, L3.2
#> 
#> From the base class: none

eta <- c(0.1, -0.2, 0.3, 0.5, -0.4, 0.2)
round(covstructs7::struct_matrix(s, eta), 4)
#>         v1      v2      v3
#> v1  1.2214  0.5526 -0.4421
#> v2  0.5526  0.9203 -0.0363
#> v3 -0.4421 -0.0363  2.0221

The sign in front of the log-determinant is the consumer’s arithmetic and not the structure’s. A gaussian written in the covariance carries \(-\frac{1}{2}\log|\Sigma|\) and one written in the precision carries \(+\frac{1}{2}\log|\Omega|\), so the structure returns \(\log|M|\) for the matrix it parametrises and lets the distribution attach the sign. The same holds for the two derivatives.


6.1.4 The inverse map
A structure also answers the reverse question: given a matrix in \(\mathcal{M}\), which free vector produces it? This is what allows a fit to be started from a sample covariance, and what allows a marginal of Section 3.5.4 to be expressed in the free values of a smaller structure.
The map is exact or refused, never obtained by optimisation. An optimisation-based inverse would return a plausible \(\eta\) for a matrix outside \(\mathcal{M}\), which is a wrong answer wearing the shape of a right one, and a caller has no way to tell the two apart. A family whose map has no closed-form inverse therefore refuses, and so does the base class on behalf of any structure that does not implement one.

m <- covstructs7::struct_matrix(s, eta)
max(abs(covstructs7::struct_free(s, m) - eta))
#> [1] 6.938894e-17



6.1.5 What a new structure has to write
Only Equation 6.1 is compulsory. A structure that implements nothing but the matrix receives numerical methods for the derivatives, the log-determinant and its derivatives, and the solve, registered on the base class exactly as the numerical fallbacks of Section 3.4 are registered for a distribution. It is therefore usable the moment it exists, and each closed form supplied later replaces the corresponding numerical method through dispatch, with no change to anything that consumes it.
The numerical derivatives obey the rule of Section 3.4: one central difference applied to the highest analytical order available, never a chain of first differences. A structure that supplies its own first derivative gets a second derivative accurate to the square root of machine precision rather than to its fourth root.
The validator check_covstruct() puts a structure through the same checks the shipped families face. It compares the derivatives against finite differences, the log-determinant against the determinant of the assembled matrix, its derivative against Equation 6.2, and the solve against a direct solution, and it reports which orders came from a closed form and which from the fallback, for the reason check_link() does: an order that comes from a fallback would otherwise be compared against a numerical differentiation of the order below, which is the same arithmetic twice and agrees however wrong the structure is.

covstructs7::check_covstruct(s, verbose = TRUE)
#> Structure: log_cholesky   (3 x 3, rank 3, 6 free)
#>   [OK         ] membership           0.00e+00
#>   [OK         ] round trip           7.77e-16
#>   [OK         ] first derivatives    2.90e-11
#>   [OK         ] second derivatives   3.67e-11
#>   [OK         ] log-determinant      2.47e-15
#>   [OK         ] logdet gradient      3.38e-14
#>   [OK         ] logdet hessian       0.00e+00
#>   [OK         ] solve and factor     3.90e-15
#>   [OK         ] shapes and names  
#>   9 passed, 0 failed, 0 not checked

title: 6  The covstructs7 package
text:
6.2 The families

6.2.1 The log-Cholesky map
The general positive definite case is parametrised through the Cholesky factor. Every positive definite \(M\) has a unique factorisation \(M = L L^\top\) with \(L\) lower triangular and \(L_{ii} > 0\), and the correspondence is a bijection. Taking the logarithm of the diagonal removes the only remaining constraint, so
\[
\eta = \bigl(\log L_{11}, \ldots, \log L_{pp},\;
             L_{21}, L_{31}, \ldots, L_{p,p-1}\bigr)
\tag{6.3}\]
ranges over the whole of \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) with \(d = p(p+1)/2\), and \(M(\eta) = L L^\top\) is onto the positive definite cone. This is the parametrisation of Pinheiro and Bates (1996). The ordering above is fixed rather than incidental: the diagonal comes first, then the below-diagonal entries column by column, and the labels of the free values follow it.
The logarithm on the diagonal is intrinsic to the map and not a swappable link. A different positive map would give a different parametrisation of the same set, but it would not compose with anything, since the constraint being removed is on the factor and not on an entry of \(M\).
Differentiating is straightforward once the factor is written as a function of the free vector. Let \(L_k = \partial L/\partial \eta_k\), which is the matrix with a single non-zero entry: \(L_{ii}\) itself in a diagonal direction, because the entry is \(e^{\eta}\), and \(1\) in a below-diagonal direction. Then
\[
A_k = L_k L^\top + L L_k^\top ,
\qquad
A_{kl} = L_k L_l^\top + L_l L_k^\top + \delta_{kl}^{\,\mathrm{diag}}
         \left( L_k L^\top + L L_k^\top \right),
\tag{6.4}\]
where the last term appears only when \(k = l\) and the direction is a diagonal one, since \(\partial^2 L/\partial \eta_k^2 = L_k\) there and vanishes elsewhere. The factor is linear in every below-diagonal free value, which is why nothing else survives the second derivative.
The log-determinant is the reason this parametrisation is comfortable. Since \(|M| = |L|^2\) and \(L\) is triangular,
\[
\log|M| = 2\sum_{i=1}^{p} \log L_{ii} = 2\sum_{i \in \mathrm{diag}} \eta_i ,
\tag{6.5}\]
which is linear in the free vector. Its gradient is the constant \(2\) in each diagonal direction and \(0\) in every other, and its Hessian vanishes identically. A term that would otherwise cost a trace per component per observation costs nothing at all.

s <- covstructs7::log_cholesky(3)
covstructs7::struct_dlogdet(s, c(0.1, -0.2, 0.3, 0.5, -0.4, 0.2))
#> log_L1 log_L2 log_L3   L2.1   L3.1   L3.2 
#>      2      2      2      0      0      0
covstructs7::struct_dlogdet(s, c(-2, 3, 0.7, -1.1, 0.4, 2.5))
#> log_L1 log_L2 log_L3   L2.1   L3.1   L3.2 
#>      2      2      2      0      0      0



6.2.2 Diagonal matrices, and where the two packages meet
A diagonal matrix with positive entries is the case in which a matrix parametrisation and a scalar link agree. The Jacobian of
\[
M(\eta) = \mathrm{diag}\bigl(h(\eta_1), \ldots, h(\eta_p)\bigr)
\tag{6.6}\]
is diagonal, which is exactly the contract a link satisfies, so covstructs7 takes \(h\) from linkfunctions7 instead of writing a positive map of its own. Any link whose range is the positive half-line serves, and its exact derivatives to fourth order come with it. The derivatives of the structure are then \(A_k = h'(\eta_k) e_k e_k^\top\) and \(A_{kk} = h''(\eta_k) e_k e_k^\top\), with every mixed second derivative zero, and the log-determinant is \(\sum_i \log h(\eta_i)\).

covstructs7::struct_matrix(covstructs7::diag_struct(3), c(0, 0.5, -0.5))
#>    v1       v2        v3
#> v1  1 0.000000 0.0000000
#> v2  0 1.648721 0.0000000
#> v3  0 0.000000 0.6065307
covstructs7::struct_matrix(
  covstructs7::diag_struct(2, link = linkfunctions7::sqrt_link()), c(1, 2)
)
#>    v1 v2
#> v1  1  0
#> v2  0  4

A single free value shared by every entry gives \(\sigma^2 I\), which is the independent case a variance component or a ridge starts from. It is the same construction with \(d = 1\).


6.2.3 A fixed matrix carried by one scale
The third family is different in kind. Here the matrix is
\[
M(\eta) = \lambda P, \qquad \lambda = h(\eta),
\tag{6.7}\]
with \(P\) a known symmetric positive semidefinite matrix and \(\lambda\) the only unknown. This is the commonest penalty in semiparametric regression: \(P\) may be the Gram matrix of a basis derivative from Section 5.3, a difference penalty \(\Delta^\top \Delta\), a neighbourhood matrix, or the identity, in which case the structure is a ridge.
Nothing here needs deriving. With the default log link, \(\lambda = e^{\eta}\) and every quantity is a constant times a function of the scale:
\[
\partial_\eta M = M, \qquad \partial^2_\eta M = M,
\]
\[
\log|M|_{+} = r\,\eta + \log|P|_{+}, \qquad
\partial_\eta \log|M|_{+} = r, \qquad
\partial^2_\eta \log|M|_{+} = 0,
\tag{6.8}\]
with \(r\) the rank of \(P\) and \(|\cdot|_{+}\) the pseudo-determinant of Section 6.3.2. The constant \(\log|P|_{+}\) is computed once at construction, since \(P\) does not change.

# a ridge: the identity, scaled
r <- covstructs7::scaled_struct(diag(4))
c(rank = r@rank, logdet_at_zero = covstructs7::struct_logdet(r, 0))
#>           rank logdet_at_zero 
#>              4              0

# a second-difference penalty on six coefficients
dm <- diff(diag(6), differences = 2)
pen <- covstructs7::scaled_struct(crossprod(dm))
c(dimension = pen@dimension, rank = pen@rank)
#> dimension      rank 
#>         6         4



6.2.4 Which side of a model a family parametrises
The name of a family does not say whether the matrix it produces is a covariance or a precision, and the two are different models. Imposing a structure on \(\Sigma\) and imposing the same structure on \(\Omega = \Sigma^{-1}\) give the same family only when the structure is closed under inversion. Diagonal matrices are, and so is compound symmetry, whose inverse is again compound symmetry with different constants. An AR(1) correlation matrix is not: its inverse is tridiagonal, which is a different pattern of zeros, so an AR(1) covariance and an AR(1) precision are genuinely different assumptions about the same data.
A structure therefore carries a label recording which side it is meant for. Nothing computed depends on it and no method reads it; it exists so that the object says what it is, and so that a consumer that cares can ask. The distribution of Section 3.5.2 takes the structure on either side and adjusts its own derivatives accordingly, which is the only place the difference has arithmetic consequences.

title: 6  The covstructs7 package
text:
6.3 Rank and the null space

6.3.1 Why a singular matrix is admitted
A covariance matrix must be positive definite for the density it describes to exist, and a precision matrix must be positive definite for the same reason: a singular covariance puts the whole distribution on a subspace, and a singular precision leaves the density unnormalisable. Both readings of a multivariate gaussian therefore require full rank, and the distribution of Section 3.5.2 refuses a rank-deficient structure.
A penalty is not a density. Writing a quadratic penalty \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\beta^\top P \beta\) as a negative log prior makes it a gaussian with precision \(\lambda P\), and the whole point of a smoothing penalty is that \(P\) is singular: its null space is the set of functions the penalty leaves alone. A second-difference penalty on a spline has the constants and the straight lines in its null space, which is what makes the penalty shrink towards a straight line rather than towards zero. That prior is improper, and its impropriety is the modelling assumption rather than a defect.
The package therefore admits rank-deficient matrices, and everything a consumer asks of one has to be redefined so that it still means something.


6.3.2 The pseudo-determinant
The determinant of a singular matrix is zero, so \(\log|M|\) is \(-\infty\) and useless. The quantity that takes its place is the pseudo-determinant, the product of the non-zero eigenvalues,
\[
\log|M|_{+} \;=\; \sum_{j : \, \nu_j \neq 0} \log \nu_j ,
\tag{6.9}\]
which is the normalising constant of the proper gaussian the penalty induces on the complement of its null space. One generic returns both, because a consumer asks the same question of either matrix — what normalising constant does this contribute — and the object knows which answer is right, through the rank it declares.
The gradient identity Equation 6.2 survives with the Moore-Penrose inverse in place of \(M^{-1}\), and for the scaled family of Section 6.2.3 it collapses to the constant of Equation 6.8.
That constant is what makes the scale estimable. The penalised objective seen as a negative log posterior contributes
\[
\frac{\lambda}{2}\,\beta^\top P \beta \;-\; \frac{r}{2}\log\lambda ,
\tag{6.10}\]
and setting its derivative in \(\lambda\) to zero gives
\[
\hat{\lambda} = \frac{r}{\beta^\top P \beta}.
\tag{6.11}\]
Dropping the second term of Equation 6.10, which is what a treatment that regards the penalty as a penalty rather than as a prior does, leaves a derivative of one sign and sends \(\lambda\) to zero. The normalising constant is therefore kept, and the rank in Equation 6.11 is the reason the rank has to be right.

dm <- diff(diag(8), differences = 2)
pen <- covstructs7::scaled_struct(crossprod(dm))
p_mat <- crossprod(dm)

set.seed(3)
beta <- as.numeric(rnorm(8))
quad <- drop(t(beta) %*% p_mat %*% beta)

# the stationary point of (lambda/2) b'Pb - (r/2) log lambda, and the same
# point found by minimising the objective numerically
obj <- function(lambda) 0.5 * lambda * quad - 0.5 * pen@rank * log(lambda)
c(closed_form = pen@rank / quad,
  numerical = stats::optimize(obj, c(1e-8, 1e8))$minimum)
#> closed_form   numerical 
#>   0.4062954   0.4063148



6.3.3 Determining the rank
The rank of a matrix is a statement about the matrix, and a numerical procedure that reads it off an assembled matrix does not always make that statement. Counting eigenvalues above a relative tolerance is the obvious route, and it fails on exactly the object this package exists to carry.
Consider a tensor-product penalty \(\lambda_1 P_1 + \lambda_2 P_2\) on a \(4 \times 8\) grid of coefficients, where \(P_1\) penalises second differences along one margin and \(P_2\) along the other. Its true rank is 28 out of 32. Counting eigenvalues of the assembled matrix above a relative tolerance gives 28 while the two smoothing parameters are comparable and 24 once they are ten orders of magnitude apart, because the contributions of the smaller term sink below the tolerance and are read as exact zeros. Smoothing parameters that far apart are an ordinary fitted model rather than a pathology, so the count is not a property of the family at all.
What is stable is the null space. The null space of a sum of positive semidefinite matrices is the intersection of their null spaces, since \(\beta^\top(P_1 + P_2)\beta = 0\) with both terms non-negative forces both to vanish. The intersection is the null space of the stacked matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} P_1 \\ P_2 \end{pmatrix}\), so the rank comes from the components, individually normalised and stacked, and never from an assembled combination. Membership of the null space is then tested against the stored basis rather than by counting eigenvalues again.

d2 <- function(k) crossprod(diff(diag(k), differences = 2))
p1 <- kronecker(d2(4), diag(8))
p2 <- kronecker(diag(4), d2(8))

count_ev <- function(m, tol = 1e-10) {
  ev <- eigen(m, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
  sum(ev > tol * max(ev))
}

# the stored null basis, and the residual it leaves in the assembled matrix
ns <- covstructs7::struct_null_basis(list(p1, p2))

ratios <- c(1, 1e4, 1e8, 1e10, 1e12)
data.frame(
  ratio = ratios,
  eigen_count = vapply(ratios, function(f) count_ev(p1 + f * p2), numeric(1)),
  stacked_rank = ns$rank,
  null_residual = vapply(ratios, function(f) {
    m <- p1 + f * p2
    max(abs(m %*% ns$null_basis)) / max(abs(m))
  }, numeric(1))
)
#>   ratio eigen_count stacked_rank null_residual
#> 1 1e+00          28           28  2.176289e-16
#> 2 1e+04          28           28  2.652472e-16
#> 3 1e+08          28           28  2.793968e-16
#> 4 1e+10          24           28  3.099442e-16
#> 5 1e+12          24           28  2.721151e-16

The count moves and the null space does not. The residual \(\lVert M N \rVert /
\lVert M \rVert\), with \(N\) the stored basis, stays at the level of rounding across the whole range, which is the statement that the four directions really are annihilated by the penalty at every combination of smoothing parameters.
The same doubt applies wherever a Cholesky factorisation is used to decide a branch. On a matrix with an exactly zero eigenvalue the pivot that ought to be zero comes out positive or negative according to rounding, so a tryCatch(chol(...)) used as a rank test answers differently on different machines for the same matrix. A verdict of that kind belongs to the eigenvalues, which describe the matrix, rather than to the arithmetic that was performed on it.


6.3.4 The solve, which a singular matrix does not have
The remaining quantity is the solve, and it is the one that is refused rather than redefined. A Moore-Penrose solve \(M^{+}B\) exists and is easy to compute, but no consumer of an improper prior asks for it. What a penalised fit inverts is \(X^\top X + \lambda P\), which is non-singular even when \(P\) is not, and which the consumer assembles from the penalty and its own design; what it asks of the penalty itself is the quadratic form \(\beta^\top P \beta\) and the log pseudo-determinant. Returning a pseudo-inverse would be a plausible matrix answering a question nobody asked, and a caller that used it would be wrong without being told.

covstructs7::struct_solve(pen, 0)
#> Error:
#> ! 'scaled' is rank deficient (6 of 8), so it has no inverse. A consumer of
#>   an improper prior needs the quadratic form and the log
#>   pseudo-determinant, not a pseudo-inverse: assemble the matrix the
#>   model actually inverts and solve that.

What the null space is for, instead, is membership. A basis of it is stored at construction, so a consumer can ask whether a coefficient vector lies in the space the penalty leaves alone — for a second-difference penalty, whether it is a straight line — without touching an eigenvalue.

n_basis <- pen@null_basis
line <- 1 + 2 * seq_len(8)
quad_of <- function(b) drop(t(b) %*% p_mat %*% b)

c(
  columns = ncol(n_basis),
  penalty_of_a_line = quad_of(line),
  penalty_of_a_curve = quad_of(seq_len(8)^2),
  line_is_in_the_null_space =
    max(abs(line - n_basis %*% crossprod(n_basis, line))) < 1e-10
)
#>                   columns         penalty_of_a_line        penalty_of_a_curve 
#>                         2                         0                        24 
#> line_is_in_the_null_space 
#>                         1





Magnus, Jan R., and Heinz Neudecker. 1999. Matrix Differential Calculus with Applications in Statistics and Econometrics. Revised. Chichester: Wiley.


Pinheiro, José C., and Douglas M. Bates. 1996. “Unconstrained Parametrizations for Variance-Covariance Matrices.” Statistics and Computing 6 (3): 289–96.


Pourahmadi, Mohsen. 2011. “Covariance Estimation: The GLM and Regularization Perspectives.” Statistical Science 26 (3): 369–87.

Six symbols are reused across chapters, without ambiguity in context, and it is better to say so than to invent notation nobody uses.
\(g\) is the link function in Chapter 2 and the gradient here; \(h\) is the inverse link throughout, and in Section 4.4.1 it is exactly that, since the map removing a box constraint is a bounded link. The two meanings of \(g\) never appear in the same section: where Section 4.4.1 needs both, the gradient is written \(\nabla f\) in full.
\(\theta\) is a parameter everywhere except Theorem 4.1, where \(\theta_k\) is the angle appearing in the theorem’s classical statement.
\(\pi\) is the zero-adjustment probability of Section 3.2.3 and nothing else. The bundle method’s aggregate subgradient, which much of the literature calls \(p\) or \(\pi\), is written \(\bar v\) here. That choice is consistent with \(v_j\) for the subgradients it aggregates, and it avoids the collision.
\(B\) is a curvature model in Chapter 4 and a design matrix in Chapter 5. The two never appear together, and both are the letter their own literature uses. For the same reason the interval of a basis is written \([a, b]\) rather than with the \(\ell\) that would collide with the log-likelihood.
\(m\) is the degree of a spline in Chapter 5, while it is a truncated expectation in Section 3.2.5 and a moment estimate in Section 4.4.2. Each carries the index its own section gives it.
\(P\) is a penalty matrix in both Chapter 5 and Chapter 6, which is the same object, and \(\lambda\) is its scale in Chapter 6 while it is a Demmler-Reinsch eigenvalue in Section 5.4. \(\eta\) is a linear predictor in Chapter 2 and the free vector of a structure in Chapter 6; both are the unconstrained coordinate an optimiser works on, which is why the same letter is right for both.
